rationale: B wins because it knows where the fact pattern ends. It writes, "whether it also uses the new on-device model, since the facts do not say so," while A turns the same hole into "A Fortune 100 manufacturer just became an early customer for Hugging Face's offline AI model." That is the difference between strategy and a phone call that dies in minute two.
gaps_in_A: "A Fortune 100 manufacturer just became an early customer for Hugging Face's offline AI model" invents a connection the update does not make; the customer is tied to the enterprise tier, not the on-device model.
"a real Fortune 100 buyer for on-device AI" repeats the same unsupported leap and makes the customer angle riskier than it needs to be.
"a quiet challenge to the cloud-inference business every major AI lab depends on" overreaches from offline capability into market-structure threat before cost, latency, or usage proof exists.
"evidence of a vendor building specifically for data-sensitive buyers" is plausible, but still dressed as conclusion; the update gives security features, not buyer motive.
gaps_in_B: "Story type: funding-mechanics" is the wrong label. This is monetization or business-model strategy, not funding.
"A Fortune 100 manufacturer is paying Hugging Face to keep its models private" is mostly grounded, but "paying" and motive should be confirmed before it becomes the headline.
Refusing "Hugging Face adds SSO and audit logs for regulated enterprises" as "duplicate" may throw away a real enterprise-security angle if the manufacturer will not speak.
"Next step: journalist-fit-check" is a shade premature; the eval configuration and customer permissions still decide which angles are pitchable.
